code.title: Generics vs ArrayList: type safety and boxing

followUps: It compiles one native body and reuses it, because all reference-type arguments are handled as a single shared form. List<string> and List<Uri> both hold only object references, which are the same size, so the JIT compiles List<__Canon> once and reuses it. Any extra type information (for a cast or typeof(T)) comes from a hidden generic dictionary passed alongside. Result: one native method for all reference types, but a separate one for List<int>, List<double> and so on.

Accept object when the value really can be anything, such as a logging or formatting argument, a dictionary of mixed property values, or a non-generic legacy API like string.Format. Also when you must store unrelated types together (a heterogeneous bag) and will pattern-match on them. If every caller passes the same kind of thing, use a generic; if a small set of types is allowed, an interface or a base class is usually better than object.

code.title: Generic constraints in action

followUps: Because the compiler needs to know how to create the type before it checks anything else: new() only makes sense on a type that is already known to be a class or struct with a base type, so the grammar requires it last. Example: where T : class, IDisposable, new() is legal; where T : new(), class does not compile. The same list order is: class or struct first, then the base class, then interfaces, then new().

For an unconstrained T, T? means "T, but may be null or default" and it adds no new type: it is just an annotation for the nullable analyzer. If T is a reference type it is a nullable reference; if T is a value type it is still plain T (not Nullable<T>), so default gives 0 for int. To get a real Nullable you need where T : struct. Example: T? Find<T>() may return null for string but returns 0 for int.

code.title: A mini hash table: buckets and entries

followUps: The key now sits in the wrong bucket, so you usually cannot find it again. Dictionary stored the hash when you inserted; if you change a field that GetHashCode uses, a later lookup computes a new hash, goes to a different bucket and returns "not found", while the old entry stays orphaned until Clear. Example: key Point(1,2) is inserted, then X becomes 9; d[new Point(1,2)] misses and so does d[new Point(9,2)]. Use immutable keys (records, readonly structs, strings).

By randomised string hashing: the default string comparer uses a per-process random seed (Marvin), so an attacker cannot craft keys that all collide. In addition, since .NET Core 3.0, Dictionary<string,T> starts with a fast non-randomised comparer and switches to the randomised one if a single bucket chain exceeds 100 collisions. Cost: a few extra operations per lookup, still O(1) average. Never pass a custom weak string hash for untrusted input.

code.title: Dictionary vs SortedDictionary vs SortedList

followUps: Use a SortedSet and call GetViewBetween, or keep the data sorted and binary search. Floor (largest value <= x): s.GetViewBetween(s.Min, x).Max; ceiling (smallest value >= x): s.GetViewBetween(x, s.Max).Min. Both take O(log n) on a red-black tree. Guard against x outside the range, since GetViewBetween throws if lower > upper. Example: set {10,20,30}: floor(25) = 20, ceiling(25) = 30. Handle empty sets and results that are empty views.

Roughly 40 to 60 bytes of overhead per entry on a 64-bit runtime. A SortedDictionary node holds the key, value, left and right references, a colour flag and an object header (16 bytes), so an int-to-int entry costs around 48 to 56 bytes compared with about 24 bytes in a Dictionary entry and 8 bytes in a SortedList (two array slots). Trees also scatter nodes in memory, so they are slower to scan than arrays. Choose SortedList when memory matters and inserts are rare.

code.title: LRU cache with Dictionary and LinkedList

followUps: Store an expiry time in each item and check it on every Get; if the item is expired, remove it and treat it as a miss. Item gets a DateTime Expires (or a monotonic tick count). Example: TTL 30 s, put at t=0; Get at t=40 returns -1 and removes the node. For memory you also need a sweep: a timer that periodically scans from the least recent end, or a min-heap keyed by expiry. Lazy checking costs O(1) per Get and the sweep keeps dead items from lingering.

Reduce how long a single lock is held or split it. Options: stripe the cache into N shards by hash(key) % N with one lock and one LRU per shard (contention drops roughly N times, but LRU becomes per shard); or make reads cheaper by recording accesses in a lock-free buffer and applying the reordering in batches, as Caffeine does. Do not use ConcurrentDictionary plus a separate list, since the two can disagree. Example: 16 shards, 8 threads, most operations hit different locks.

code.title: Priority ties: why you add a sequence number

followUps: There is no built-in way, so the standard way to "update priority" is lazy: push a new entry with the new priority and keep a dictionary of the current priority per item; when you dequeue an item whose priority does not match, skip it as stale. Cost is O(log n) per push and extra memory for stale entries. If you need true decrease-key, write your own indexed heap that keeps a position map from item to array index and sifts up or down, also O(log n).

A 4-ary heap is shallower, so it does fewer cache misses. With 4 children per node the height is log base 4 of n, half that of a binary heap, and the four children sit next to each other in the array (often one cache line). A pop compares up to 4 children per level, but fewer levels and fewer memory jumps usually win. Example: 1,000,000 items is 20 levels binary versus 10 levels 4-ary. Push is slightly faster too, as it sifts up fewer levels.

code.title: Removing from a List safely while looping

followUps: Yes in the sense that it keeps the relative order of survivors: RemoveAll walks the list once, copying the items that stay to the front in their original order, then trims the tail. The items it removes are not visited again, so the predicate runs once per item. So [1,2,3,4,5,6] with an "is even" predicate becomes [1,3,5]. Note this is about order of kept items; the word "stable" is more often used for sorting, and List.Sort is not stable.

Another thread changing a List while you enumerate is a data race, and it may or may not throw. The version check catches some cases, but it is not guaranteed because List is not thread-safe: you can skip items, see one twice, or hit a corrupted internal array. Fix it by locking around every access (including the whole foreach), taking a snapshot copy under a lock (lock(l) copy = l.ToArray()), or using a concurrent or immutable collection. A ConcurrentDictionary enumerates safely without throwing.

code.title: IComparable vs IComparer vs IEqualityComparer

followUps: Wrap the lambda in a small class or use Comparer<T>.Create. For ordering: Comparer<Person>.Create((a, b) => a.Age.CompareTo(b.Age)), which returns an IComparer you can pass to Sort or SortedSet. For LINQ you can use OrderBy(p => p.Age) and skip the comparer. There is no built-in factory for IEqualityComparer, so write a tiny class with two lambdas or use a record-like key. Example: list.Sort(Comparer<Person>.Create((a, b) => b.Age - a.Age)) sorts oldest first (watch overflow with subtraction).

Sorted and hash collections give inconsistent results. If CompareTo says two items are equal (0) but Equals says false, a SortedSet treats them as duplicates and silently drops one, while a HashSet keeps both. Example: compare people by Age only: adding Ann(30) and Bob(30) to a SortedSet leaves 1 item. The reverse, equal objects with a non-zero CompareTo, makes Contains and Remove miss them. Also GetHashCode must be equal for items that Equals treats as equal, or HashSet breaks.

code.title: Static fields are per closed generic type

followUps: A generic dictionary is a small hidden table of runtime type handles that shared code reads to learn the exact types. Because all reference-type instances share one body (List<__Canon>), operations that need the real T, such as new T[n], typeof(T), casts to T or calling a static method, look up the handle at run time. The slot is fetched from the method or class's dictionary (a couple of memory loads) and cached. Value types avoid this because each has its own native code with T baked in.

A generic virtual method has its own type arguments that are only known at the call, so the runtime cannot put it in a fixed virtual table slot. Each call must resolve the target using the object's type plus the method's type arguments, via a dictionary lookup that is cached, then call through a stub. A normal virtual call is one indirect jump; the generic one adds that lookup and may be 5 to 10 times slower in a tight loop. Avoid generic virtual methods in hot code; prefer generic classes or non-virtual helpers.

code.title: Generic math stand-in with a struct calculator

followUps: They are operations that throw OverflowException when a result does not fit, written checked in a generic algorithm. C# 11 adds the interface members operator checked + (and -, *, ++, casts) to the numeric interfaces. Under checked(a + b) or a checked context the compiler calls the checked version; otherwise the plain one wraps around. Example: for byte, checked(200 + 100) throws while unchecked gives 44. A type like INumber<T> carries both, so generic code behaves like ordinary int code.

The call is resolved at compile time per closed type, and the interface method is static, so there is no object and no virtual table. In T.Zero or a + b with where T : INumber<T>, the JIT builds code for the real type argument (int, double, ...) and binds the static member directly, even inlining it. Example: T.Zero becomes a constant 0 for int. For shared reference-type code, the runtime uses the generic dictionary to find the target. Static abstract members can be used only through a type parameter, not through an interface-typed variable.

code.title: List enumerator is a struct; the interface boxes it

followUps: Each LINQ operator wraps the source in a new iterator object, so a pipeline such as Where().Select().ToList() allocates one object per stage plus the delegates, and each element passes through interface calls. A Where on a List with a lambda that does not capture a variable allocates the iterator and one cached delegate. Cost per query is a handful of small objects; per element it is zero extra allocation unless the lambda captures state (then a closure object is created once). In hot loops a plain for loop avoids all of it.

The compiler turns an yield return method into a hidden class that implements IEnumerable and IEnumerator. Calling the method allocates one object holding the locals and a state number; the first GetEnumerator call on the same thread reuses that same object, so a single foreach costs one allocation total, not one per element. A second simultaneous enumeration allocates another copy. Captured variables live as fields on it. So iterating 1,000,000 items by yield return is still 1 allocation, plus the interface call per MoveNext.

code.title: Fast membership: HashSet vs sorted array

followUps: Choose ImmutableHashSet when you need to create modified versions cheaply while old versions stay valid, for example snapshot-style state, undo history, or lock-free updates with ImmutableInterlocked.Update. Adding to it creates a new set that shares most of its tree with the old one, O(log n) time and few new nodes. FrozenSet cannot be changed at all, so each change would mean rebuilding all one million items. If the set never changes, use FrozenSet; if it changes occasionally and readers want a stable snapshot, use ImmutableHashSet.

Build it on a background task and swap it in when ready, and make callers handle the not-ready period. For example, Lazy<Task<FrozenSet<string>>> started at startup, with await on first use; or load from a file with a streaming reader and call ToFrozenSet once on a thread-pool thread. Since a one-million-string freeze may take hundreds of milliseconds, never do it inline in a request. Publish via a volatile field so all threads see the finished set, and keep the old one in use during a reload.

code.title: A bad GetHashCode makes Dictionary slow

followUps: Write a BenchmarkDotNet test that uses the same key shape and the same number of keys, then compare the bad and fixed key types. Fill a Dictionary with, say, 100,000 keys where many share one tenant id, then time 100,000 lookups. Use [Params] for the number of keys and a [MemoryDiagnoser]. Also count Equals calls in the test (a static counter, as in the program above): 2000 same-hash keys gave about 2,000,000 Equals calls versus 2,000 for a good hash. Run in Release mode with realistic data, not random numbers that hide the clustering.

Under concurrency a plain Dictionary is unsafe: concurrent writes can corrupt it or even hang a lookup in an infinite loop, and slow lookups make that window larger. Use ConcurrentDictionary (fine-grained locks, lock-free reads) or, for read-mostly data, build a new FrozenDictionary or immutable snapshot and swap the reference. Also a long chain now means a long time inside a lock. Fix the hash first; then pick the structure. Example: 8 writers on one Dictionary can lose entries or throw.

code.title: Order book with SortedDictionary and LinkedList

followUps: Because money and prices need exact comparison and exact map keys, and floating point cannot give that. Doubles cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so two prices that should be equal may differ in the last bit and land on different levels, and rounding errors accumulate. Decimal is exact but slower (about 10 times) and 16 bytes. A long in ticks (price 101.50 with tick 0.01 becomes 10150) compares in one instruction, hashes cheaply, and is exact. Convert to a display value only at the edges.

Read the first key of the sorted structure, or cache it. A SortedDictionary gives it in O(log n) by Keys.First() (a walk to the left-most node), not O(1). To get true O(1), keep a field bestBid that you update when a level is added or emptied: on add, bestBid = max(bestBid, price); when the best level empties, find the next one in O(log n) once. Another option is an array indexed by tick offset with a pointer to the best level that moves only a few slots, which is O(1) in practice.
